La fin du PEQ laisse des milliers d’immi: The end of the PEQ leaves thousands of immigrants in limbo, jeopardizing their future in Quebec and the promises that brought them here.
Un manifestant tient une pancarte sur la: A protester holds a sign at Place de la paix. Photo credit: Charline Caro
La semaine dernière, le gouvernement Leg: Last week, the Legault government announced a new immigration plan that includes a reduction in the number of people admitted, as well as program restrictions and cuts.
Au cours de la préparation de cet articl: While preparing this article, I sought out people affected by these measures, in particular by the abolition of the Quebec Experience Program (PEQ), which allowed immigrants to obtain permanent residence almost automatically after several years of studying or working in Quebec.
La détresse est grande parmi les nouveau: Distress is running high among newcomers, hundreds of whom are sharing their dismay on social media or with community organizations. The uncertainty is total: these people were counting on the PEQ when they came to Quebec, after leaving behind their country, their jobs and their families.
<strong>Le gouvernement Legault a annonc: The Legault government has announced the elimination of the Quebec Experience Program (PEQ), which made it easier for immigrants who graduated or worked in Quebec to obtain permanent residence. After investing many years in Quebec believing they could settle here, thousands of people and their families now face increasingly precarious status, and even a possible return to their country of origin.
Le grand sourire d’Amine n’est pas heure: Amine’s broad smile isn’t a happy one, but a bitter one. The dark circles under his eyes reveal the long nights he has spent without sleep, choked by stress and anger, as “the Quebec government is destroying [his] family.”
En appel vidéo depuis son salon, le père: On a video call from his living room, the father of three takes a deep breath. When he opens his eyes again, he says he is ready to talk about the “nightmare” he has been living since the announcement of the new immigration restrictions, with the provincial government planning to lower its immigration thresholds from 60,000 this year to 45,000 in 2026.
Amine est arrivé au Québec il y a deux a: Amine arrived in Quebec two years ago with his wife and their three children. They left Morocco, where they were happy, he says with a nostalgic smile. “We had a stable life, a house, a car.”
« Un jour, on entend parler des Journées: “One day, we hear about Journées Québec,” he continues calmly, referring to the Quebec government’s foreign worker recruitment program. Officials from the Ministry of Immigration had even travelled to Morocco to attract local workers to the Belle Province. The father saw a great opportunity for his children, who would get a “better life” and a “globally recognized education.”
Les parents hésitent, mais sont vite ras: The parents hesitated, but were quickly reassured by the guarantees on offer. “From day one, we were promised that a program, the PEQ, would allow us to stay in Quebec permanently,” Amine says, his voice growing shakier.
La famille marocaine « accepte le défi »: The Moroccan family “accepted the challenge” and left for Quebec in August 2023, after being selected. “I sold everything I owned. I quit my job, I closed my bank account,” Amine lists. “Everything I had as a life, I put in 25-kilo suitcases to be here in Canada,” he says, in a mix of hope and regret.
Les manifestants montrent leurs pancarte: Protesters show their signs to passersby and the media on hand. Photo credit: Charline Caro
Le programme sur lequel comptait Amine e: The program that Amine and his family were counting on to settle permanently in Quebec is the Quebec Experience Program (PEQ). It was the fast track to a Quebec Selection Certificate (CSQ), the step toward obtaining permanent residence. To qualify, immigrants had to hold a Quebec diploma and have one year of work experience, or two years of experience without a diploma, in addition to having a command of French.
La semaine dernière, le gouvernement pro: Last week, the provincial government announced the end of this program, leaving newcomers in uncertainty, with nothing to guarantee they will be able to stay once their work permits expire in a few months.
La seule option qui s’offre à eux pour o: The only option now available to them for obtaining authorization to settle in Quebec is the Skilled Worker Selection Program (PSTQ), a harder and less certain path, because this program gives the government more control over the selection of permanent immigrants.
Le PSTQ fonctionne selon un système de p: The PSTQ works on a points system based on a set of criteria, such as education, work experience, sector of activity, geographic location and knowledge of French. Unlike the PEQ, the PSTQ does not guarantee selection even if you meet a certain number of criteria.
De plus, les résidents de la région de M: What’s more, residents of the Montréal region will be at a major disadvantage, because the new plan calls for cutting immigration to the metropolis first in order to redirect it to the regions. Applying through the PSTQ while living in Montréal could therefore considerably reduce the chances of being selected, judging by the latest announcements.
Pour Yamanda Bouchaala, membre de l’équi: For Yamanda Bouchaala, a member of the team organizing a protest against the elimination of the PEQ, the PSTQ amounts to a lottery. “The chances of getting permanent residence are now very slim, even impossible for some,” she explains. “And if you’re not drawn, you’ll have to pack your bags and leave,” she adds, still in shock.
L’autre option pour obtenir la résidence: The other option for obtaining permanent residence is to move to another Canadian province and apply there through Express Entry, as long as the work permit is still valid. While French speakers are favoured by this program, there is no guarantee that this approach will succeed.
Cheveux noués, visage inquiet, Lina, 35: Hair tied back, face worried, Lina, 35, paces around her apartment during our call. Like Amine, she left everything behind with her husband to come to Quebec, after Ministry of Immigration officials recruited them in Tunisia. He was a restaurateur, while she was a senior director at a Tunisian-German company.
Like Amine, Lina was given promises. “They told us about the PEQ and permanent residence. They told us about Quebec and the good life,” she says with an ironic laugh.
Zied*, lui, est arrivé à 19 ans pour étu: Zied*, for his part, arrived at 19 to study, planning to build his life in Quebec. Sitting in his gaming chair, the Polytechnique graduate sets his phone down in front of him to keep his hands free. “I’ve lived here for seven years, seven years of dreams and plans,” says the man, who now works as a software engineer at a bank.
« Ces personnes-là ont tout investi au Q: “These people invested everything in Quebec, thinking they could stay,” says Yamanda Bouchaala. “They put in time, money, everything!”
Les yeux dans le vide, Zied calcule le c: Staring into space, Zied calculates the total cost of his studies. “$14,000 a semester… That’s $125,000 in all,” he says, looking incredulous.
Amine, lui, a investi toutes ses économi: Amine has put all his savings into setting up his family in Montréal and spends his entire minimum-wage salary on rent every month. “I agreed to start over at the bottom of the [pay] ladder,” he says, though he was a department head at a telecommunications company in Morocco.
Lina, pour sa part, a eu de grandes diff: Lina, for her part, had great difficulty finding a job. With her credentials unrecognized, she had to take a position that doesn’t match her qualifications. A law graduate in her thirties, she was finally hired as an educator at a school in Quebec City. “I don’t want to use this word, but for me it was a ‘fall,’ a demotion,” she says.
Pour Zied et Lina, le plus gros sacrific: For Zied and Lina, the biggest sacrifice remains having left their families behind in Tunisia. The young woman recalls the good and bad moments she has missed, such as her father’s heart surgery. She pauses, her eyes welling up with tears.
Si l’arrivée au Québec fut pour elle « t: While arriving in Quebec was “very, very hard” for her, she says that a month ago she was finally starting to adapt and to be happier in her new life. “Even when my family called me, I was more enthusiastic,” says the woman, who left them reluctantly.
« Ici, j’ai mes amis, mes souvenirs, mes: “Here, I have my friends, my memories, my activities and my habits,” says Zied. “I’ve lived here for seven years, Quebecers tell me I’m one of them […], and my employer tells me he needs me,” he says proudly.
Le rêve québécois a brusquement pris fin: The Quebec dream came to an abrupt end last week, when the Legault government abolished the program that allowed immigrants to obtain permanent residence after a few years of studying or working. “Everything has changed. Life has turned dark,” says Amine curtly, his broad smile gone. “We have two options: either leave, or leave.”
Pour obtenir la résidence permanente, l’: To obtain permanent residence, the option facing immigrants is therefore to move to another city or province and apply through another program, a move with no guarantee of success. “Leaving Montréal or leaving the country, it comes down to the same thing,” says Zied, who will have to “start over from scratch” either way. “I’m going to go to an English-speaking province, when I speak French, I have a job and my whole life is here?” the young man wonders.
« Si on rentre en Tunisie, qu’est-ce qu’: “If we go back to Tunisia, what can we do? We no longer have a house, a car, or savings,” says Lina, who left everything behind barely two years ago.
« Les enfants refusent catégoriquement d: “The kids flatly refuse to leave. They’ve only just integrated,” says Amine. His “little ones,” as he calls them, no longer speak Arabic, the language of their country. “Going back will be fatal for them,” the father whispers, his eyes moist.
Membre du mouvement citoyen contre la su: A member of the citizens’ movement against the elimination of the PEQ, Yamanda Bouchaala condemns the CAQ government’s brutal measure. “We came following the rules, we had rights, and now we have nothing,” she says bluntly.
Après le choc de l’annonce vient le stre: After the shock of the announcement comes the stress. The work permits of Lina, Amine and Zied expire in two months, six months and one year respectively, and none of them knows what to do to extend their time in Quebec.
« Je ne dors plus, j’arrive même pas à v: “I can’t sleep anymore, I can’t even live normally…” says Amine, who thinks constantly about his children, whose “lives are going to be destroyed,” he believes. And after the stress comes the anger: “Quebec got me! What they’ve done to all these people is awful!” the father erupts.
« C’est pas acceptable, c’est pas accept: “It’s not acceptable, it’s not acceptable!” Zied repeats over and over, refusing to lose everything after seven years of life in Quebec. “They give us hope, and in the end, they tell us: ‘We don’t want you anymore, actually.’”
« Je le dirais haut et fort : le gouvern: “I’ll say it loud and clear: the government deceived us,” Lina says indignantly. “They broke our lives,” she continues. She adds that she would have preferred that “they leave [her] alone” in Tunisia, rather than come recruit her. “We are not furniture or objects, we are human beings!” she exclaims, her voice breaking, before hanging up.

Lundi matin, une manifestation a lieu à: On Monday morning, a protest takes place in Montréal in front of the Ministry of Immigration, Francisation and Integration to denounce the abolition of the PEQ. Participants answered the call of a citizens’ movement supported by the organization Le Québec c’est nous aussi.
Des centaines de personnes sont présente: Hundreds of people are present, and some take the microphone to tell their stories, similar to those of Amine, Zied and Lina: years spent studying or working in Quebec believing they could settle here.
Malgré la détresse ambiante, la foule de: Despite the prevailing distress, a wave of hope sweeps through the crowd of protesters when the possibility of a transition is mentioned. Yamanda Bouchaala clings to that possibility: “Of course we believe in it, we’re going to make our voices heard. Me, I’m convinced that we have our place in Quebec.”
